title: The Moon illusion
hook: The rising Moon looks huge, yet it is the same size as when it is overhead.
peek: A full Moon on the horizon can look enormous. Photographs show it is no bigger than when it rides high in the sky, and it is actually a little farther away. The swelling happens in your head.
lede: A full Moon rising over rooftops can look startlingly large. Yet a photo taken at the horizon and another taken hours later overhead show a Moon of the same size. At the horizon it is in fact slightly farther from you, by roughly the Earth's radius, so it looks about 1.5% to 2% smaller. People have puzzled over this for over 2,000 years.

bullets.text: A common belief is that the air magnifies the low Moon like a lens. It does not. Refraction near the horizon slightly squashes the Moon from top to bottom, making it smaller, not bigger.

Ptolemy discussed the Moon illusion in the second century AD, and around 1000 AD the Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham argued it came from how we judge distance, an idea that still shapes modern explanations.

One leading theory is that we see the sky as a flattened dome, with the horizon farther away than the zenith. An object of fixed size that seems farther away looks bigger. Researchers still disagree on the full answer.
Looking at the low Moon through a rolled-up paper tube, so that the landscape is hidden, usually makes it look ordinary again. That supports the idea that the horizon scenery feeds the illusion.
